meta.subtitle: Scenario 72 — The Word 'Minimal' (a fictional composite)
meta.summary: A permanency report calls a mother's compliance 'minimal' — her folder says 22 of 24, a finished course, and 24 of 26 visits — and fifteen days to turn numbers into findings.
meta.title: The First 90 Days

body: Your name is Deanna Fenn. Your son Ravi is seven. He has been placed with a foster family since Monday, June 15, 2026, after a neglect adjudication tied to your untreated depression and the services you missed while you were disappearing into it.

Today the county agency's court report for the first permanency review arrives ahead of the hearing. Most of it is dates you recognize. One word is not: your compliance with the plan, the report says, has been "minimal."

Here is the thing about a court report: the judge reads it first, before anyone speaks, and a report is not a decision. At the review, the court itself must make determinations — from evidence — and an adjective in a report is only an adjective until evidence makes it something more. The review is Tuesday, December 15, 2026. You have fifteen days to find out what your evidence is.

choices.note: By the third page your underline has become a list. Lists can be checked. That is their power.
choices.text: Read the report a second time, underlining every sentence you think is wrong

choices.note: She is in court until four. Her voicemail is not the enemy — but the folder on your counter might be your best witness, and it is already home.
choices.text: Call your lawyer before you read another word of it

nodes.title: The Word in the Report

body: Your folder — the one you have kept on the kitchen counter since June, adding a page after every appointment — tells a different story than the adjective. Therapy: 22 of 24 sessions, with attendance slips. Parenting course: completed, certificate in a plastic sleeve. Drug screens: all negative, results clipped together. Visits with Ravi: 24 of 26.

The two missed visits were in September, the two weeks your bus route was suspended and the replacement shuttle never came to your stop. You called the visit line both times. You wrote that down, too — the dates, and the name of the woman who answered.
Numbers are not findings. But numbers are what findings are made from — if they ever reach the judge in a form the judge can use.

choices.note: One page, four numbers, no adjectives. It looks, you notice, nothing like the report — and exactly like the folder.
choices.text: Write the numbers on one clean page: 22 of 24, course complete, 24 of 26

choices.note: She will want it either way. What she does with it is the next fifteen days.
choices.text: Take the whole folder to your lawyer, as it is, tabs and all

nodes.title: What the Folder Says

body: Ms. Park, your lawyer, spreads the report and your one clean page side by side. "This review exists because the law schedules it," she says. "A permanency hearing is held within six months of removal — Ravi was placed June 15, and December 15 is inside that window. (42 Pa.C.S. § 6351(e)(3)(i))"

"At that hearing, the court — not the report — determines four things: whether placement is still necessary, whether you complied with the permanency plan, whether you have made progress toward alleviating the circumstances that caused placement, and whether the agency made reasonable efforts to finalize the plan. (§ 6351(f)(1),(2),(3),(5.1)) Every one of those is a finding the judge makes out loud, from evidence."

"'Minimal' is not one of the determinations," she says. "It is a word in a document. Our job is to make sure that when the judge makes the real determinations, the judge is looking at numbers — not at the word."

choices.note: "Their visit logs," she says. "Written by their workers, after every visit. You have never seen them. You are allowed to."
choices.text: Ask what evidence the agency's own file might already hold about you

choices.note: "You can," she says. "Judges hear 'unfair' every day. What they can act on is a record. Let's go get the rest of yours."
choices.text: Ask whether you can simply tell the judge the word is unfair

nodes.title: What a Determination Is

body: Every visit you have had with Ravi since June, a worker sat in the corner and wrote notes afterward: what you brought, how he settled, how the goodbye went. Those notes live in the agency's file. So do the attendance records the agency itself received, and the caseworker's own running log — the raw material the word "minimal" was supposedly built from.

The regulation is plain about that file: the record "shall be released upon request." (55 Pa. Code § 3130.44(d)) And it is not to be read to protect agency employees' privacy as a basis for withholding it. (§ 3130.44(f)) A request, Ms. Park says, should be written, dated, and kept — a phone call asks; a letter proves you asked.
Without those logs, December 15 is your word against the report's word. With them, it might be the agency's own file against the agency's own adjective.

choices.note: One page, one stamp, one copy for the folder. The cheapest power in this entire system, exercised in writing.
choices.text: Sign and send the written request for the agency record, keeping a dated copy

choices.note: She is pleasant about it. Pleasant is not a paper trail, and nothing about the call will ever prove what was asked for, or when.
choices.text: Ask the caseworker by phone to 'send over whatever you have on visits'

nodes.title: The File You Have Never Seen

body: The request goes out Wednesday, with your case number on it and Ms. Park copied. Her copy goes in a new section of your folder labeled, in her handwriting, REQUESTS — PROOF.
"Now we wait for the file to answer," she says. "Files answer slowly. That's why we asked on day two and not day fourteen."
Meanwhile, life in this case does not pause for mail. Saturday is a visit.

choices.note: He is on chapter nine. Somebody in a corner will write down that you brought the book. After today, you know exactly who, and you have asked to read it.
choices.text: Go to Saturday's visit with Ravi's reading book, as always

choices.note: The visit is never ordinary to Ravi. The folder will keep. The book, chapter nine, will not read itself.
choices.text: Spend Saturday organizing the folder instead, and let the visit be ordinary

nodes.title: A Request With a Date On It

body: The caseworker is kind on the phone. "I'll pull what I can," she says, "things are backed up." There is no date in that sentence. There is no list in it either — visits? screens? everything? — and by Friday you cannot remember exactly what you asked for, which is precisely the problem Ms. Park warned about.
Nothing in the conversation was written down by anyone whose job is to keep it. If a packet ever comes, it will come on the agency's schedule, in the agency's selection.
Saturday is a visit either way. The case does not pause for the mail that may not be coming.

choices.note: Chapter nine. A worker writes something in the corner. Whether you ever get to read it is now a matter of somebody's goodwill and memory.
choices.text: Go to Saturday's visit with Ravi's reading book, as always

choices.note: True, and it will matter. It is also the only paper you will be able to control from here on.
choices.text: Spend Saturday organizing the folder instead — your own paper is the paper you control

nodes.title: "I'll Pull What I Can"

body: The visit room has the couch, the toy shelf, and Ravi, who has grown out of his shoes again and wants you to know he noticed it first. You read chapter nine, and most of chapter ten, because stopping mid-chapter is, in his jurisprudence, not allowed.

In the corner, the visit worker writes. You find yourself wondering — the new, permanent wondering of this case — what today's sentence will be. Engaged? Distracted? Whatever it is, it will be in a file a judge may read, phrased by someone who watched you for one hour.
After the goodbye, Ms. Park's text is waiting: time to build the exhibit packet. "Bring everything," she writes. "We are going to make your folder into something a court can take."

choices.note: Building, it turns out, is a verb with rules: copies, tabs, an index — and nothing handed up that a clerk cannot mark.
choices.text: Meet Ms. Park Monday to build the packet

choices.note: Her reply is one line: "Judges rule on what is offered and admitted. Folders are not offered. Exhibits are. Come Monday."
choices.text: Ask whether the judge can just look through your folder at the hearing

nodes.title: Chapter Nine

body: Ms. Park lays it out at her office table. An exhibit gets into a hearing by being offered: handed up, marked by the clerk, admitted or refused on the record. That means copies — one for the judge, one for agency counsel, one for the file — organized in the order the numbers will be argued: attendance first, certificate, screens, visits.
The copying costs $15 you were saving for Ravi's new shoes. The alternative costs nothing: bring the originals in your tote bag and hope the judge leafs through them at the bench.
"Judges do not take tote bags into evidence," Ms. Park says. "Originals in a bag are still a bag. Copies with an index are an offer waiting to happen."

choices.note: Fifteen dollars of copies. The folder becomes a packet: numbered, spare copies in front, ready to be handed up and marked.
choices.text: Copy and organize the packet — certificates and attendance, tabbed and indexed

choices.note: They are real. Reality, in a courtroom, is a property conferred by being offered and admitted — and a tote bag offers nothing.
choices.text: Bring the originals in the tote bag — they are the real documents, after all

nodes.title: Copies, Tabs, an Index

body: The packet sits on Ms. Park's table, tabbed and indexed, with two tabs still empty on purpose. One is labeled VISIT LOGS — AGENCY FILE. One is labeled TRANSIT — SEPTEMBER.
"An index with empty tabs is a promise we intend to keep," she says. "Whatever fills them has to arrive as paper, from the people who keep it."
Today is mail day. What is in your mailbox depends on what you did on December 2.

choices.note: Thick envelopes move at their own speed. This one was requested in writing, with a date on it.
choices.text: Check the mailbox before you do anything else

choices.note: "Look for the visit logs," she says. "Not a summary of them. The logs themselves, with the workers' own words."
choices.text: Call Ms. Park first and ask what to look for when it comes

nodes.title: A Packet With Empty Tabs

body: The tote bag holds everything: the original certificate in its sleeve, the attendance slips, the screen results, your handwritten September notes riding under a bus pass and a grocery list. It is all true, all yours, and all — in the only sense a hearing recognizes — unorganized and unoffered.

Ms. Park looks at the bag the way mechanics look at an engine in a shopping cart. "We will do what we can with it," she says, and does not say the rest: that 'what we can' has a ceiling, and the ceiling is low.
Today is mail day. What is in your mailbox depends on what you did on December 2.

choices.note: If the agency's own logs are coming, they are coming to a mailbox — not to a tote bag.
choices.text: Check the mailbox before you do anything else

choices.note: On top of a bag is still in a bag. Rearranging is not offering, and December 15 will not pause for it.
choices.text: Rearrange the tote so the certificate is on top, where the judge would see it first

nodes.title: Everything, in a Bag

body: The mailbox holds the usual weather of a life: a flyer, a bill, and — depending on a Wednesday decision — an envelope from the county agency, or the absence of one.
What happens next was decided on December 2, in the difference between a letter and a phone call.

addHidden: File — visit logs released on written request (§ 3130.44(d)): 'engaged, prepared' × 24
choices.note: Released on request, as the regulation says. The agency's own words, about your own visits, in your own hands.
choices.text: Open the agency's envelope — the record you requested in writing is here

choices.note: A phone promise keeps no schedule. The logs exist — in a file you cannot quote, in words you have never been shown.
choices.text: Check the empty mailbox a second time, and go in without the logs

nodes.title: Mail Day

body: The visit logs are better than you hoped, because they were not written for you. Visit after visit, in different workers' handwriting: "engaged, prepared." "Brings Ravi's reading book; he settles quickly." "Prepared snack; knew his school schedule." Twenty-four visits of it.

And the two September dates are there too — noted as missed, with the worker's own line underneath: "Mother called ahead; bus route suspended, no shuttle." The agency's file knew about the bus. The agency's report, which called all of this "minimal," apparently did not read the agency's file.
Ms. Park slides the logs into the empty tab. "Now it is not your word against their adjective," she says. "It is their file against their adjective. Judges notice that arithmetic."

choices.note: "Proof from your providers," she says. "Your therapist sent a letter. Letters are the next problem."
choices.text: Ask Ms. Park what is still missing from the packet

choices.note: "Called ahead; route suspended." Four words from a worker who was there. Worth more, on December 15, than anything you could say about September yourself.
choices.text: Read the September log entries one more time before the packet closes

nodes.title: Engaged, Prepared

body: There are no logs to read, because there was no dated, written request to answer. Somewhere, in a file you cannot see, twenty-four visits have sentences attached to them. You do not know what the sentences say. On December 15, neither will the judge — unless the agency chooses to read them aloud, in its own selection.
You know what you did at those visits. Knowing is not the same as showing, and a hearing runs on showing.
Ms. Park is brisk, not unkind. "Then the packet is what we have. Let's strengthen what we can still reach — your providers."

choices.note: "Records," she says. "Your therapist sent a letter. Letters are the next problem — for everyone, with or without logs."
choices.text: Ask Ms. Park what your providers can still give the packet

choices.note: "You can, and you may have to. A parent's memory against a report's adjective is a fair fight only in the sense that both sides get to speak. Paper was the equalizer. We go with what we have."
choices.text: Ask whether you can describe the visits to the judge yourself, from memory

nodes.title: Her Word Against the Adjective

body: Your therapist has written a warm letter: you are engaged, you are doing the work, your depression is being treated and responding. Ms. Park reads it twice and sets it down gently, the way you set down something fragile that will not bear weight.

"A letter cannot be cross-examined," she says. "Which sounds like a virtue, until you realize it also cannot be believed the way a witness or a record can. The agency's lawyer will call it advocacy. What a court can weigh is the attendance record itself — dates, stamps, the provider's own log — or the therapist, briefly, in person."
Getting the records takes a release, a call from counsel, and a provider's office that answers its fax. The letter takes nothing. That is exactly the difference between them.

addHidden: Exhibit — therapy attendance record (22 of 24) and parenting certificate, marked and admitted
choices.note: The provider's own log: 22 of 24, each date stamped, the two absences in October marked 'called ahead — ill.' Records do not need to be warm. They need to be records.
choices.text: Have counsel arrange the provider's attendance records — dates and stamps, not adjectives

choices.note: It does say everything. It can prove almost nothing: no dates a judge can count, no record a clerk can mark, no one to answer a single question about it.
choices.text: Bring the therapist's letter as it is — it says everything, in kind words

nodes.title: The Letter Problem

body: The attendance records arrive the way real evidence usually does: unglamorously, by fax, slightly crooked. Twenty-four scheduled sessions down the left margin. Twenty-two attendance stamps. Two October dates marked in the provider's own hand: "called ahead — ill."
The parenting provider's completion record comes with it — the certificate's official twin, the one that lives in a system instead of a plastic sleeve.

Ms. Park adds them to the packet behind the attendance tab. "Twenty-two of twenty-four is now a document," she says. "On Tuesday it can become a finding. That is the whole alchemy of this work, and it is not glamorous, and it is everything."

choices.note: One page, in an appendix, rating 'service engagement: low.' She has been saving it for last because it is the quietest problem in the file — and quiet problems are the ones judges never hear about.
choices.text: Turn to the last piece Ms. Park flagged: the scored summary stapled to the report

choices.note: "Almost," she says. "There is one page in their report we have not answered yet. Unanswered pages have a way of answering themselves — badly."
choices.text: Ask whether the packet is finished now

nodes.title: Dates and Stamps

body: The letter goes into the folder exactly as written: two warm paragraphs, a signature, a phone number nobody will call from a bench. What it does not contain is a single countable thing — no session dates, no attendance count, nothing a judge could turn into a finding about compliance or progress.

Ms. Park does not argue. "Some judges will read it," she says. "None of them can build a § 6351(f)(2) compliance finding out of 'doing the work.' Findings are built from numbers and records. We will argue it for what it is."
One problem remains either way: the scored summary stapled to the back of the agency's report.

choices.note: It is one line in an appendix. It is also, Ms. Park says, the line most likely to be quoted back at you if nobody answers it in writing.
choices.text: Turn to the scored summary — the appendix page rating engagement 'low'

choices.note: "Two pieces of paper do not cancel," she says. "One of them is an unanswered form. The other is an unverifiable letter. The form is winning that exchange, and we have four days to change it."
choices.text: Ask whether the letter at least cancels out the summary

nodes.title: Kind Words, No Dates

body: The report's last page is a scored summary — a form that sorts the case into categories. One line reads: "Service engagement: low." Underneath, in the attendance data it was scored from, your two September missed visits are counted as refusals. Not as a suspended bus route. As refusals — the worst available word, chosen by arithmetic nobody checked.

Ms. Park is careful about the remedy, and you should hear the care: the court rules provide for presenting evidence and argument to rebut a provision of a scored summary, and for challenging factual errors in it. (Pa.R.J.C.P. 1340(E), (F)) But whether Rule 1340 reaches a scored assessment summary has NOT been tested in a published opinion — it is an argument counsel makes, not a settled right. A written rebuttal, filed through counsel before the hearing, puts the correction in the court's hands either way. Hoping the judge does the appendix math herself costs nothing.
"She won't," Ms. Park says. "Judges read reports. Appendices are where errors go to be adopted."

addHidden: Rebuttal — scored summary's attendance error answered in writing (Rule 1340(E)/(F) — untested)
choices.note: Two pages: the two September dates, 'refusal' struck through by documentation, filed before the hearing and stamped. The argument is flagged as untested — and the correction is in the file regardless of how the argument fares.
choices.text: File the written rebuttal through counsel, correcting the attendance error with the dates attached

choices.note: The math is in an appendix, behind a summary line that reads cleanly. Unnoticed math is how 'low engagement' survives a hearing nobody lied at.
choices.text: Leave it — the judge will surely notice the math doesn't work

nodes.title: The Error in the Appendix

body: The rebuttal is filed Friday afternoon: the scored summary's attendance line, the two September dates, and the correction, in writing, through counsel. (Pa.R.J.C.P. 1340(E), (F)) Ms. Park repeats her caution on the walk out — whether Rule 1340 reaches a scored assessment summary has NOT been tested in a published opinion — "and that is why we filed paper instead of relying on the rule. If the judge takes the argument, the correction is argued. If she doesn't, the correction is still in front of her, attached to the packet."
One question is still coming on Tuesday, and both of you know it. The judge will ask about the two missed visits directly — judges always ask about the worst dates personally.
There is a piece of paper in the world that answers that question better than you can. It is at the transit authority.

choices.note: A route suspension is a public fact with a custodian, a letterhead, and dates. Public facts can be handed up. Memories cannot.
choices.text: Go after the transit authority's letter about the suspended route

choices.note: Rehearsal helps you. It does not create the document. She books the rehearsal — and raises an eyebrow that does the rest of the arguing.
choices.text: Ask Ms. Park to rehearse your answer about September instead

nodes.title: Filed, Stamped, Answered

body: Nothing is filed. The scored summary keeps its clean, wrong line — "service engagement: low" — and the attendance data that produced it stays where it was put: in an appendix, unexamined, waiting to be read aloud by agency counsel as if it were a finding instead of a form.
Ms. Park closes the report without comment. Some fights are lost in the decision not to have them, and she has learned not to relitigate a client's Friday on a Friday.
One question is still coming on Tuesday either way: the judge will ask about the two missed September visits directly. There is a piece of paper, at the transit authority, that answers it.

choices.note: Whatever else went unanswered, September can still be documented. A suspended route is a public fact, and public facts have letterhead.
choices.text: Go after the transit authority's letter about the suspended route

choices.note: Your words are true. The question is what Tuesday does with true words that arrive without paper — you have seen, by now, exactly what it does.
choices.text: Plan to explain September yourself, in your own words, when the judge asks

nodes.title: The Line That Survives

body: The transit authority suspended your route for eleven days in September — a bridge inspection, a notice in the paper, a sign zip-tied to your stop. The two missed visits fall squarely inside those eleven days. All of that is documented, somewhere in a municipal file, by people who keep records for a living.
A letter confirming the suspension dates can be requested in writing and picked up, or faxed to Ms. Park, in time to sit inside the packet behind the tab marked TRANSIT — SEPTEMBER.
Or Tuesday can be the day you explain a bridge inspection from memory, to a judge who has heard a thousand explanations and admitted none of them.

addHidden: Exhibit — transit authority letter: route suspended the two missed dates
choices.note: Letterhead, a route number, and the exact suspension dates — matching the two missed visits to the day. September, documented by the people who suspended it.
choices.text: Request the transit authority letter in writing and get it into the packet

choices.note: It counts as testimony, weighed against a written report, by a judge deciding what she can find. You have watched that weighing happen to warmer things than a bus story.
choices.text: Explain it yourself on Tuesday — you lived it; that should count

nodes.title: The Letter at the Transit Office

body: The letter arrives on transit letterhead: the route, the reason, and the suspension window — which contains your two missed visit dates the way a frame contains a picture. Ms. Park puts it behind the last tab without ceremony, which you have learned is her ceremony for things that matter.

The packet is complete: attendance with stamps, a certificate with a record behind it, screens, the agency's own visit logs saying "engaged, prepared," and a municipal letter explaining the only two numbers anyone will argue about.
Tomorrow night there is nothing left to gather. There is only the question of what, exactly, to ask for.

choices.note: Findings are sentences a judge says out loud. Asks that cannot be said in one sentence each rarely become them.
choices.text: Spend Sunday night on the asks — what you want the judge to say, in her own findings

choices.note: Rest is also a strategy, and the packet is genuinely built. But a hearing has a last five minutes, and what gets asked for in them has a way of becoming what gets ordered.
choices.text: Try to rest — the packet is built; Tuesday will be what it will be

nodes.title: The Last Empty Tab, Filled

body: Sunday night, you rehearse September: the sign on the stop, the shuttle that never came, the calls you made to the visit line. It is all true, you tell it well, and it remains — as Ms. Park puts it, not unkindly — a story you will tell a judge who is holding a written report that calls those same two dates refusals, in a scored summary nobody corrected.
She does not push. The transit office will still exist after Tuesday. Letters requested after a hearing, she notes, answer questions the hearing has already decided.
Tomorrow night there is one task either way: deciding what, exactly, to ask for.

choices.note: A parent who knows her three asks cold can survive a hard five minutes. A parent with a speech usually cannot.
choices.text: Spend the night on the asks — what you want the judge to say, in her own findings

choices.note: Smooth is not the same as documented. But it is what you have chosen to bring, and you will bring it as well as it can be brought.
choices.text: Rehearse September once more, start to finish, until it is smooth

nodes.title: September, From Memory

body: Ms. Park makes you write the asks the way a judge would have to say them, because that is the test: a finding is a sentence spoken on the record. Three asks survive her editing, each one sayable in a single breath.

One: a finding, under § 6351(f)(3), that you have made substantial progress toward alleviating the circumstances that caused placement — the depression treated, the services done. Two: unsupervised day visits, named in the order as the next step. Three: the next review date, set from the bench, so progress has a deadline instead of a hope.
"If it can't be said in one sentence," she says, "it can't be ordered in one either. Learn these three. Sleep. Tuesday, the paper talks first — then, if the judge asks, you do."

choices.note: A progress finding. A named next step. A date. Three sentences, memorized the way Ravi memorizes chapters.
choices.text: Learn the three asks until each fits in one sentence, exactly as a judge would say it

choices.note: It is heartfelt and four pages long. Judges make findings out of sentences, not speeches — but the feeling in it is real, and it will be in the room with you.
choices.text: Write out a longer statement about everything since June, to read if you get the chance

nodes.title: Asks You Can Say in One Sentence

body: The courthouse at 8:40 has the particular quiet of places where other people's worst days are scheduled in half-hour blocks. Ravi's case is third on the list. His foster mother has brought him to the children's room down the hall; you saw his backpack go past the door.
On counsel's table: either a tabbed packet with spare copies, or a tote bag with everything you own in it, depending on decisions that are now two weeks old and completely finished being changeable.

Ms. Park straightens the papers — or the bag — once. "The report talks first," she says. "Then the evidence talks. Then the judge decides what the determinations are. Remember which of those three you control: the middle one."

choices.note: Fifteen days of paper, distilled into a morning. Whatever the packet holds is what the morning holds.
choices.text: Sit down, breathe, and let the hearing come in its own order

choices.note: "That," she whispers back, "is the entire plan. It has always been the entire plan."
choices.text: Whisper to Ms. Park, one last time: 'Make sure she sees the numbers'

nodes.title: The Morning of the Review

body: The agency's case is the report, presented the way reports are: the caseworker summarises, agency counsel holds the paper up like a flag, and the word lands where it was aimed. "Compliance," counsel says, "has been minimal. Service engagement is rated low. Placement remains necessary, and the goal should be reviewed if progress remains minimal."

The judge is looking at the report. Then, for the first time, she looks at your side of the room. This is the moment the whole fifteen days were for: what your counsel does next — offers evidence, or argues adjectives — is the hinge the determinations will swing on.

The court will determine continuing necessity, compliance, progress, and the agency's reasonable efforts. (§ 6351(f)(1),(2),(3),(5.1)) It will determine them from whatever is actually in front of it in the next twenty minutes.

choices.note: The clerk marks them. The judge turns, for the first time today, away from the report — toward documents with your numbers and their handwriting on them.
choices.text: Counsel offers the packet and the agency's own visit logs — exhibits, handed up and marked

choices.note: It is an unfair word. The argument about it takes eleven minutes, produces no exhibit, and leaves every number in the room exactly where it started: unspoken.
choices.text: Argue that 'minimal' is an unfair word for everything you have done

choices.note: Whatever form your evidence takes — a tote bag, a letter, your own voice — this is the version of it the judge will have when she asks her questions.
choices.text: Offer what you have, as you have it, and answer for the rest from the chair

nodes.title: The Agency Presents 'Minimal'

body: The judge asks you two questions directly, the way Ms. Park promised she would. They are not hostile. They are worse than hostile: they are specific.
"Ms. Fenn, the two missed visits in September. Tell me about those." And then: "The original circumstances were untreated depression and missed services. What, concretely, is different now?"

Behind your counsel, the answer to the first question either exists as a transit authority letter inside an offered packet, or it exists as your explanation, weighed against a written line that calls those dates refusals. The answer to the second either points to stamped attendance records and the agency's own logs — or to a warm letter and your voice. You answer both questions as well as what you brought allows anyone to answer them.

choices.note: Dates are the dialect findings are written in. Yours either match documents the judge is holding, or they don't — she is checking, in real time, which.
choices.text: Answer with dates: the suspension window, the calls ahead, the treatment record, session by session

choices.note: Every word is true, and the judge does not doubt a syllable of it. Love, however, is not one of the four determinations — and the clock on the wall is not moved by it.
choices.text: Answer from the heart: how hard you have worked, and what Ravi means to you

nodes.title: Two Questions From the Bench

body: The judge gathers the report, and whatever else the morning put in front of her, and begins the part of the hearing that is the hearing: the determinations, spoken on the record — continuing necessity of placement, compliance with the plan, progress toward alleviating the original circumstances, and whether reasonable efforts were made to finalize the plan. (§ 6351(f)(1),(2),(3),(5.1))

A report's adjective cannot survive contact with admitted numbers — or it can sail through untouched, if the numbers never arrived in a form the court could use. Which of those happens now was decided, piece by piece, across fifteen days of stamps, copies, faxes, and one letter that was or was not sent.
She looks up. What she says next becomes the order.

addHidden: Order — finding under § 6351(f)(3): substantial progress toward alleviating the original circumstances
choices.note: This order exists because every piece of it was in the room as paper: logs requested in writing, exhibits offered, records instead of a letter, an error answered, September documented.
choices.text: The court finds substantial compliance and substantial progress, and orders the next step

choices.note: Numbers reached the judge, but something the win needed did not — the logs, the records, the rebuttal, the letter for September — and an unanswered line or an unoffered page caps what she can find.
choices.text: The court improves the findings — 'moderate' — but orders no step

choices.note: With nothing offered in a form the court can take, the only findings available to adopt are the ones the agency brought. Courts adopt what is in front of them.
choices.text: The court adopts the report's findings as its own

nodes.title: The Determinations, Said Aloud

body: The written order arrives Wednesday, and you read the findings the way you once read the report — except that this time the words were earned in a room you were in. Under § 6351(f)(2): substantial compliance with the plan. Under § 6351(f)(3): substantial progress toward alleviating the circumstances that caused placement. The goal remains reunification. And the next step is not a hope but an order: unsupervised day visits, beginning before Christmas, with the next review date set from the bench.

Ravi is not home tonight — a permanency review was never going to do that in one morning, and nobody honest promised it would. But the file that follows him into the next hearing no longer contains the word "minimal" as its summary of you. It contains findings, made by a court, from the agency's own logs and your providers' own records.
The word in the order is "substantial." You put the order in the folder, in front of the report, where it belongs.
debrief: WHAT THE FILE SAID — The record the court actually saw: visit logs released on written request under § 3130.44(d) describing Deanna as 'engaged, prepared' across 24 visits; a therapy attendance record (22 of 24) and parenting certificate, marked and admitted as exhibits; a written rebuttal answering the scored summary's attendance error (Rule 1340(E)/(F) — untested); a transit authority letter placing the route suspension over the two missed dates; and the resulting order, with a finding under § 6351(f)(3) of substantial progress. The scored summary's 'low engagement' line was scored from attendance data that counted the bus-cut visits as refusals — it survived only until somebody answered it in writing.

THE LAW THAT CONTROLLED — At a permanency hearing the court determines, from evidence, the continuing necessity of placement, compliance with the permanency plan, and progress toward alleviating the original circumstances (§ 6351(f)(1),(2),(3)), and whether reasonable efforts were made to finalize the plan (§ 6351(f)(5.1)). A report's adjective is none of those determinations. Evidence controlled the outcome only because it was offered — handed up, marked, admitted — and the agency's records were in the room because they 'shall be released upon request' (55 Pa. Code § 3130.44(d)). The Rule 1340 rebuttal carried its flag to the end: whether that rule reaches a scored assessment summary has not been tested in a published opinion.

WHAT NO STRATEGY CONTROLS — A different judge could have weighed the same packet more grudgingly; a different worker could have written thinner logs; the transit letter could have taken three weeks instead of four days. Ravi remains placed tonight, and the next review will be its own morning with its own weather. This outcome is a set of findings, not a verdict on Deanna as a mother — outcomes in this system also turn on workers, judges, resources, and luck. What the fifteen days changed was narrower and more durable: when luck was handed something to work with, it was paper.
nodes.title: The Record Says Otherwise

body: The judge's findings improve on the report — genuinely. Compliance is found "moderate." Progress is "noted." The word that will follow this case into its next hearing is a better word than the one it arrived with.

But placement continues unchanged. No step is ordered — no unsupervised visits, no expansion, nothing with a date on it except the next review itself. Something the morning needed never fully arrived: the agency's own logs unquoted, a warm letter where attendance records should have been, the scored summary's "low engagement" line still standing in the file unanswered, or September explained in a voice instead of documented on letterhead. The judge found as much as the paper in front of her allowed, and not one finding more.

Ms. Park writes the date of the next review on the folder in pencil. "'Moderate' is not the end of this," she says. "It is the starting line of the next fifteen weeks. We know, now, exactly which paper was missing."
debrief: WHAT THE FILE SAID — Some of Deanna's numbers reached the court as exhibits, and the findings moved exactly as far as the offered paper: compliance upgraded from 'minimal' to 'moderate,' progress noted. What capped the morning was whichever piece stayed unoffered or unanswered — visit logs never obtained on a written request under § 3130.44(d), a therapist's letter standing in for attendance records, the scored summary's 'service engagement: low' line surviving because its attendance error (the bus-cut visits counted as refusals) was never rebutted in writing under Rule 1340(E)/(F) — untested — or the transit documentation that never joined the packet. The file, as always, rated what it could see.

THE LAW THAT CONTROLLED — The court still made its own determinations under § 6351(f)(1),(2),(3),(5.1) — continuing necessity, compliance, progress, and reasonable efforts to finalize the plan — but a permanency court can only determine from the evidence offered to it. Findings follow paper: a letter is not an attendance record, an appendix error unanswered is an error adopted, and 'moderate' is what 'substantial' becomes when one load-bearing document is missing. The goal remains reunification, and the next permanency hearing comes within six months of this one (§ 6351(e)(3)(i)) — the fight is continued, not lost.

WHAT NO STRATEGY CONTROLS — The judge's temperament, the caseworker's drafting, the transit authority's mail room, and plain timing all held pieces of this outcome, as they hold pieces of every outcome in this system; workers, judges, resources, and luck are co-authors no parent can edit out. 'Moderate' is a measurement of a record on one Tuesday, not a measurement of a mother. The missing paper, unlike the missing luck, can still be gathered — and the next review will read a file that this review has already changed.
nodes.title: 'Minimal' Becomes 'Moderate'

body: The judge adopts the report's findings — the phrase takes four seconds to say, and it is the whole hearing. Compliance: minimal. Engagement: low. Placement: continued, on the same terms, with agency counsel adding, almost gently, that the goal may need to change "if progress remains minimal" by the next review.

Your certificates existed the whole time. Your attendance happened. The visits happened, twenty-four of them, with a reading book. None of it was in the room in a form a court could take: the originals sat in a tote bag under the counsel table, the agency's own logs were never obtained, the scored summary's error was never answered, and a form's adjective walked into an order without meeting a single document on its way.

Outside, Ms. Park does not dress it up. "The case is not over," she says. "But understand what happened in there, because it is the whole lesson: evidence that is never offered does not lose. It never plays."
debrief: WHAT THE FILE SAID — The court saw the agency's report and its scored summary, essentially unaccompanied: 'compliance: minimal,' 'service engagement: low,' the two September missed visits recorded as refusals in attendance data nobody corrected. Deanna's contrary paper never became evidence — the therapy record and parenting certificate stayed unoffered in a tote bag, and the agency's own visit logs (obtainable on written request under 55 Pa. Code § 3130.44(d), where workers had written 'engaged, prepared') were never in the room to contradict the adjective they were summarised by. The file rated what it could see, and what it could see was the report.

THE LAW THAT CONTROLLED — A permanency court's determinations — continuing necessity, compliance, progress, reasonable efforts (§ 6351(f)(1),(2),(3),(5.1)) — are made from evidence, and evidence exists at a hearing by being offered, marked, and admitted. A court handed only one side's paper will adopt that paper's findings; that is not bias, it is arithmetic. The agency floating a goal change is not itself an outcome — the goal remains reunification unless and until a later court orders otherwise, and any termination petition, if one ever came, would require the agency to prove its grounds by clear and convincing evidence. But the next review, within six months (§ 6351(e)(3)(i)), now starts from 'minimal' as a court's finding rather than a report's adjective — a harder place to start, built entirely from an empty offer.

WHAT NO STRATEGY CONTROLS — Judges differ, workers differ, and a sterner or kinder morning was always possible; outcomes in this system turn on workers, judges, resources, and luck alongside anything a parent does, and this ending is a map of missing paper, not a verdict on Deanna's worth or Ravi's bond with her. What can be said plainly is the mechanical part: every document that would have changed this hearing existed on December 15 — in a kitchen folder, in an agency file, in a transit office. None of it was in the only place evidence lives. The next record starts at the next review, and it has not been written yet.
